overview.text: El Greco (1541–1614), born Domenikos Theotokopoulos on Crete, was a Greek-born painter who made his career in Spain, especially Toledo. After working in Venice and Rome, he settled in Toledo, where religious commissions, portraits, and unusual landscapes became central to his work. His art draws on his training in Byzantine icon painting and Italian Renaissance art, but its striking Mannerist style is recognized by elongated, twisting figures, forceful gestures, lively brushwork, and dramatic, sometimes unreal colors. He painted visionary religious scenes as well as perceptive portraits; his rare landscape View of Toledo presents the city as an expressive, rearranged vision rather than a strictly literal record. Later artists, including Picasso, admired his work.

key_facts.text: “El Greco” means “the Greek” in Spanish; his birth name was Domenikos Theotokopoulos.
Born in Crete, he traveled to Venice and Rome before settling in Toledo, Spain, in the late 1570s.
His Toledo commissions included religious works such as The Disrobing of Christ, also known as the Espolio.
The Burial of Count Orgaz depicts a church tradition about Saints Stephen and Augustine appearing to help bury the count, alongside a vision of heaven.
View of Toledo, painted around 1600, is a rare landscape in his body of work; its expressive treatment of the city reflects his artistic interpretation rather than strict naturalism.
Elongated, twisting forms and vivid, unconventional colors distinguish his style; Picasso was among the later artists who admired him.
